context: New techniques. Our new idea is a pipelining technique: as more vertices become irrelevant in the current phase, we can start running the next phase on these vertices, concurrently with the current phase which has not necessarily finished completely. In our algorithm, after starting phase (` − 1), we wait for O(1) MPC rounds and then start phase `. There are O(log log ∆) phases in total, each taking O(log log n) MPC rounds, so the round complexity is O(log log ∆) · O(1) + O(log log n) = O(log log n) in total. Our pipelined algorithm produces exactly the same result as the unpipelined version does (using the same random bits). When running phase `, we need to deal with pending vertices that have not finished their computation in previous phases 1, 2, . . . , ` − 1. As it is still unknown whether they will be removed by the start of phase `, the messages sent from these vertices during phase ` are temporarily marked as pending. If a vertex receives a pending message, then its state also becomes pending, and so on. Now we take a closer look at what happens when we perform graph exponentiation. In the ideal scenario, after phase ` − 1 completely finishes, the maximum degree drops below `−1 ∆`−1 := ∆1/2 , allowing us to store the (δ log∆`−1 n)-hop neighborhood of a vertex into the local memory. However, in the actual situation, when expanding the neighborhood we may encounter pending vertices, which may not have degree upper bounded by ∆`−1 . It would be problematic if we simply excluded these vertices when we expand the neighborhood, as they may later have degree reduced to the interval (∆` , ∆`−1 ] and become relevant in phase `. So we have to store them as well, and this poses challenges to bounding the local memory and the global memory of our algorithm – this is the most technical part of our analysis. In this overview, we provide some intuition on how we analyze the global memory used for storing the neighborhoods. We will analyze the neighborhoods of non-pending vertices and of pending vertices separately. In phase `, after repeating the LOCAL algorithm k times, the number of non-pending vertices v with degrees in (∆` , ∆`−1 ] can be bounded by n/∆k`−1 . The d-hop neighborhood (we will maintain d = ck for some constant c ∈ (0, 1)) of such a non-pending vertex v only contains vertices u with degree at most ∆`−1 , since otherwise u would still be waiting for phase ` − 1 to finish, causing v to become a pending vertex. Hence the total size of d-hop neighborhoods of these non-pending vertices v is roughly at most (n/∆k`−1 ) · ∆d`−1 < n. Now we consider the pending vertices. For any pending vertex v, it must be within k distance from a vertex u which is currently stuck at phase ` − q, for some q ≥ 1. We pick such u with the biggest q, so v can be reached from u by a k-step path on which all vertices have degree ≤ ∆`−q (since if any of them had degree greater than ∆`−q , it would be stuck at a phase earlier than ` − q, contradicting the maximality of q).
